qt: to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) Subject:
In the EU, 8.3 times more people die from the cold than from heatwaves.

In 2024, the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre published data showing that, on average, 363 809 people die each year in Europe as a result of the effects of the cold and around 43 729 people as a result of the effects of heatwaves. There are, therefore, 8.3 times as many cold-related deaths as heat-related ones per year. Cold weather is thus the greatest temperature-related health problem in the EU. Nonetheless, the EU Mission on Adaptation to Climate Change focuses mainly on heat, droughts, heavy rain and floods. There is, however, no specific strand dealing exclusively or primarily with the health effects of cold temperatures. What is more, experts are concerned that the EU’s energy and climate policies, as well as the sanctions against Russia and the war in Iran, could lead to energy shortages in the coming autumn and winter, which could in turn create massive problems for the heating of homes. 1.
What measures will the Commission take to finally reduce the catastrophic number of cold-related deaths?
Why are there no comparable emergency plans to prevent cold-related deaths, as there are for heatwaves?
What measures will the Commission take to prevent a further increase in the number of cold-related deaths in the EU in the face of an impending energy shortage this autumn?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (23.11.2026) The cold-related deaths estimated in the study1 cover all natural causes of death associated with low temperatures, including cardiovascular and respiratory diseases, which helps explain why the estimates are considerably higher than heat-related deaths. In 2025, the Commission published the Union prevention, preparedness and response plan for health crises2 to promote an effective and coordinated response to cross-border health threats, including climate-related risks. The Preparedness Union Strategy3 further strengthens this approach by recognising cold waves among the relevant risks and promoting an integrated all-hazards approach. Regulation (EU) 2022/23714, in place since 2022, aims to improve preparedness for and response to serious cross-border health threats, amongst others, through early warning and response systems and risk assessments5, while the Health Security Committee6 supports coordination between EU/EEA7 countries. The EU is diversifying its energy supplies, increasing interconnections, advancing electrification and promoting homegrown clean energy to reduce vulnerabilities linked to fossil fuel dependencies. The Commission and Member States continuously monitor the energy security situation, including through the winter outlooks8 on gas supplies and electricity adequacy, and act, if necessary, in a coordinated manner. In addition to preventing cold-related deaths, the EU must also become much better prepared for the growing health threat of extreme heat. The Commission presented an EU Framework for Climate Resilience on 27 October 20269, and the President of the Commission announced10 the development of a European Heatwave Plan for better early warning systems and health preparedness.
